LESSON 1 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

What Is Cyber Security?

A beginner's guide to cyber security: what it protects, what outcomes it defends, who does the work, and how the major security frameworks organise it.

Beginner14 min
Why this matters

Cyber security is the practice of protecting systems, networks, data and people from damage and misuse. It is not a single product you install. It is a set of decisions about what matters, what could go wrong, and how much effort each risk deserves.

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.

  1. Verification: Keep a written inventory of the assets that actually matter to you.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Every asset you rely on - a laptop, a database, a payment API, an employee account - has an owner, a value and a lifetime.
  • Threats are the parties and events that could cause harm: attackers, malware, accidental mistakes, hardware failure, and insiders.
  • Vulnerabilities are the weaknesses those threats exploit. A system with no known weakness is not a safe system; it is an unexamined one.
  • Controls reduce risk. Some prevent an attack, some detect it, some limit the damage after it happens.
  • Security work is a loop: identify what matters, test what could break, apply controls, then verify the controls still work.

The background

  • Security existed long before computers: locks, guards, accounting and physical safes protected the same three things we now call confidentiality, integrity and availability.
  • As computing moved onto shared networks in the 1980s and 1990s, the problem shifted from protecting one machine to protecting many connected ones.
  • The internet made that harder still, because identity became hard to establish and the number of remote users grew without bound.
  • Organisations now publish structured guidance so that security is repeatable rather than folklore: the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the CIS Controls, and the OWASP Top 10 are widely used references.

Real-world examples

  • A hospital loses record availability when a backup cannot be restored, and patients feel it as cancelled appointments rather than as a security incident.
  • A retailer treats payment card numbers as the assets that matter most, and invests in segmentation and monitoring to protect them.
  • A small charity is targeted by the same automated credential-stuffing traffic as a large bank, because attack tooling is cheap and automated.

What to look for

  • Write down what you are protecting and who would be harmed if it were unavailable, altered, or disclosed.
  • Notice where trust is granted automatically, because unexamined trust is where most incidents begin.
  • Ask what would happen if this component failed, and whether anyone would notice within minutes or within months.
  • Distinguish a bug from a security issue: it only becomes security-relevant when it crosses a boundary someone was supposed to control.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Keep a written inventory of the assets that actually matter to you.
  • Prioritise by impact, not by how interesting a control is to implement.
  • Prefer boring, well-understood controls over clever ones you cannot maintain.
  • Test your defences deliberately, in a way that is authorised and safe.
  • Treat recovery as a security control: backups, tested restores and rehearsed downtime plans.
